column2: On the authority of Abū Hurayrah (may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace) said: “Every joint of a person owes a charity every day on which the sun rises:

judging justly between two people is a charity; helping a man with his mount, lifting him onto it or lifting his belongings onto it, is a charity; a good word is a charity; every step you take towards the prayer is a charity; and removing something harmful from the road is a charity.”
Sulāmā (“joint”): with ḍammah on the undotted sīn, a light lām, and the short final alif; it means the joints.
It is established in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim that they are three hundred and sixty.
ʿAlayhi (“owes”): the pronoun is masculine though it refers to a feminine noun, in consideration of the meaning, namely the mafṣil (joint).
Ṣadaqah (“a charity”): in return for what Allah has blessed him with in those joints, for had He willed He would have taken away their ability, and He would be just in doing so.

So their being kept for him requires constant gratitude by giving charity, for if he lost a single bone, or it stiffened, or would not stretch or bend, his life would be disrupted and his affliction would be great; and charity wards off affliction.
“On which the sun rises”: he added this qualification lest it be thought that “day” here means a long period, as one says “the Day of Ṣiffīn”,
which was many days,
or time in general, as in the verse: “On the day it comes to them, it will not be averted from them” [Hūd 11:8].
“Judging justly between two people”: two who bring a case for judgement, two disputants, or two who have cut each other off,
“is a charity”: to them both, for protecting them from the ugly words and deeds that result from quarrelling.
“Lifting him onto it”: as he is, or helping him to mount.
“A good word”: remembrance [of Allah], supplication for oneself and others, and addressing people with what brings joy, unites hearts and brings them together.
Khaṭwah (“step”): with fatḥah on the khāʾ, a single stepping; with ḍammah (khuṭwah), the distance between the two feet.
Tumīṭu (“removing”): with ḍammah on its first letter; putting aside.
Al-adhā (“something harmful”): whatever harms passers-by: filth, impurity, stones, thorns and the like.

The structure of the human being's bones and their soundness are among the greatest blessings of Allah the Exalted upon him, so each bone needs a charity given for it in particular, in order to complete gratitude for that blessing.

Persevering in voluntary deeds every day, and that an act of worship done on one day does not suffice for another day; so one should not say, for example: I did it yesterday, so it suffices me today, because he ﷺ said: “every day on which the sun rises”.
Charity is not confined to wealth.
The virtue of reconciling between people.
Urging attendance at the congregational prayers and walking to them, and thereby filling the mosques; for if he prayed at home, he would miss the reward mentioned in the hadith.
The printed text reads إذ لو لى في بيته فإنه الأجر, evidently for إذ لو صلى في بيته فاته الأجر (“for if he prayed at home, he would miss the reward”).
Encouragement to remove harmful things; included in its meaning are widening roads that are narrow for passers-by and moving those who buy and sell in the middle of public roads.
By the favour of Allah the Exalted, a little good earns much reward.
